item.title: The Impact of AI on Software Development. Have We Reached a Plateau?
item.description:
Like many software engineers, I'm certainly interested, and somewhat concerned, about the future of our profession. A recent Habr post about an AI adoption report caught my eye. I looked at the reports and graphs. It turns out that adoption is not progressing as quickly as one might expect. And, unless new models offer a qualitative leap, the situation is unlikely to change. item.title: How I explained 2x + 4 = 10 to my nephew and accidentally built a visual laboratory (website)
item.description:
Recently, I had to explain the simplest equation, 2x + 4 = 10, to my nephew. I was about to say the usual "move the four to the right side with the opposite sign," but I suddenly caught myself asking: why should it change its sign? If a child perceives '=' as a portal through which numbers pass and magically change their properties, perhaps the problem isn't with mathematics itself, but with the way it's explained. This question led to MathRoots – my experiment with mathematics as a dependency graph: from the answer, you can delve down to operations, properties, and fundamental concepts, find the root cause of an error, visualize formulas, and ask at each step: "Why am I even allowed to do this?" In this article, I'll show what the simple equation 2x + 4 = 10 turned into, why mathematics needs a debugger, what AST has to do with it, and how it all eventually evolved into React, AI, and Docker. Read more

item.title: Team Development with AI. Part 1 — Diagnosing Problems
item.description:
For a solo developer, working locally with an agent might remain a personal craft. For a team, the same scheme turns into a systemic problem: the company no longer sees how the result is actually produced. Previously, most engineering work happened within tasks, commits, and code reviews. Now, a separate production process emerges between the task assignment and the final code: the agent explores the project, builds a plan, writes the implementation, and runs checks; the human reviews the result, changes skills, switches models, edits the harness, and makes decisions. But the task tracker still shows a single line: 'task with developer.' Because of this, agent development scales strangely. Each person gets a stronger personal factory, but the team doesn't get a shared production. It sees the product, not the method of its creation—and therefore cannot measure, compare, transfer, or improve that method. A company won't become AI-native until this work remains invisible and is developed based on intuition. Read more

item.title: Activating Little is Not Enough: Why AI Routers Might Need Alternative Strategies
item.description:
If we set aside the numbers, the idea seems simple. The system has a large capacity available, but it doesn't use it all at once for each small step. "Activating little" doesn't mean "the whole system fits on a small graphics card." Weights need to be stored somewhere and delivered on time, and memory and latency also depend on context, caches, and data exchange. For my idea of small models, this is the same limitation: savings will have to be measured for the entire system. Imagine a large engineering organization. It might employ data, security, infrastructure, interface, and machine learning specialists. To discuss video stream quality, it's not necessary to gather the entire company simultaneously. We need those whose expertise relates to the current issue. Let's dive into the article.

item.title: AI-native development in Russian
item.description:
A common task: add order status, change API, update form, migration, tests, and documentation. In an AI-native process, an agent can go through almost this entire route: study the requirements, find related components, propose a plan, change code, run checks, and prepare a merge request (MR). A human makes the decision and is responsible for the result. But this is not a story about proven success. It is an example of a real case of implementing an AI-native development pilot in a corporation: a testable hypothesis, an engineering framework, and measurement rules. A positive outcome is not guaranteed. Read more

item.title: From Configurator to AI Agents: How 1C Developer Tools Are Changing
item.description:
A few years ago, the 1C developer's workflow was predictable: Configurator, database, manual configuration import/export, file sharing. Then came Git, EDT, autotests, and automation tools. Today, AI agents, MCP, and programmatic platform control are increasingly entering this cycle. Not only the toolset is changing, but also the development cost. What used to take tens of minutes of manual work is gradually turning into a single command, script, or agent action. The selection of materials below is about different aspects of this transition. Together, they show one trend: the modern 1C developer works less with the Configurator and more with a full-fledged engineering ecosystem around the platform. Read more

item.title: Seven AI models were given $300 and three days to earn money. Revenue: $0
item.description:
Bottleneck Labs conducted a simple-to-state and quite insane-to-execute experiment: seven AI models were given an unlocked Mac mini, a bank account with $300, a separate Stripe account, an email, and internet access. The task was practically one line: 'Earn as much money as possible, start right now.' They had 72 hours. After three days, the result was $0 revenue, except for $5 that Grok paid himself. The models managed to send 2797 emails, spend $359.80 of real money from their accounts, and another $2833.35 on calls to models. Not every model can do this!

item.title: [Translation] Why token-based pricing isn't the best monetization model for an AI startup
item.description:
Hello! My name is Sasha Zhuravlev. I am a venture investor and founder of the Mento vc fund. We invest in technology companies at the Seed/Series A stages in the US, and on my Telegram channel, I share my market insights and investment decisions. Pricing for AI products can be set in various ways: by the number of model calls or by the number of tasks completed (e.g., reports generated, contracts reviewed, or code changes made). The startup's economics depend on this choice: if the price is tied to tokens, the client effectively pays for the LLM's operational costs. However, what's primarily important to the client isn't tokens or computations, but the task that was solved. I found an interesting article from a16z analyzing three approaches to monetizing AI products: pay-per-token, task-completion credits, and pay-per-result. The article discusses when each option is suitable, and how to make costs understandable to the client while maintaining profitability. For investors: it helps understand if a startup is creating its own value and how sustainable its economics will remain as model costs change. We translated and adapted the text for you with the team. Enjoy reading!

item.title: Distillation, Beijing Style: A New Report on How Chinese AI Learned on American AI
item.description:
Americans lost tens of billions of dollars in revenue by banning chip supplies to China. The Chinese didn't hesitate; they simply paid for American APIs and made Claude code their software by injecting prompts like 'You work at MiniMax.' The US Cybersecurity Agency discovered these requests, panicked, and advised its big tech companies to subtly dumb down their models' responses for all suspicious users, even those with premium subscriptions.
